summary: This Wikipedia-derived note is a broad overview of New York City, covering its history from the 1624 Dutch trading post to the present, its size and metropolitan area, and its role as a global center of finance, media, culture, sports, and immigration. It also summarizes the city's government, transit, parks, schools, public libraries, economic inequality, demographics, and notable disasters and historic sites. The source repeats some paragraphs with updated figures, so population numbers appear for both 2016 and 2017.
one_line: Overview of New York City's history, population, economy, culture, sports, government, transit, and landmarks as the most populous U.S. city.
key_facts: New York City traces its origin to its 1624 founding in Lower Manhattan as a trading post by colonists of the Dutch Republic, and was named New Amsterdam in 1626.
The City of New York had an estimated 2017 population of 8,622,698 over a land area of about 302.6 square miles (784 km).
More than 12 million European immigrants were received at Ellis Island between 1892 and 1924.
The New York metropolitan area had an estimated 20.3 million people in its 2017 Metropolitan Statistical Area and 23.7 million residents in its Combined Statistical Area.
Bill de Blasio, the first Democrat to serve as mayor since 1993, was elected in 2013 with over 73% of the vote and assumed office on January 1, 2014.
New York City has not been carried by a Republican in a statewide or presidential election since President Calvin Coolidge won the five boroughs in 1924.
The New York City Subway had 469 stations in operation, and nearly the entire system remains open 24 hours a day.
The Port Authority Bus Terminal serves 7,000 buses and 200,000 commuters daily, making it the busiest bus station in the world.
The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in 1911, the city's worst industrial disaster, took the lives of 146 garment workers.
The steamship General Slocum caught fire in the East River in 1904, killing 1,021 people on board.
The Battle of Long Island, the largest battle of the American Revolutionary War, was fought in August 1776 entirely within modern-day Brooklyn.
The City Council is a unicameral body of 51 council members, and the mayor and council members serve four-year terms with a three consecutive-term limit.
New York City is supplied with drinking water by the protected Catskill Mountains watershed, and it is one of only four major U.S. cities whose drinking water mostly does not require treatment.
In 1664, Peter Stuyvesant, Director-General of New Netherland, surrendered New Amsterdam to the English without bloodshed, and the English renamed it New York after the Duke of York.
The New York City Public Schools system serves about 1.1 million students in more than 1,700 primary and secondary schools.
